Conformity. The tendency of individuals to align their behavior, beliefs, or judgments with those of a group, even when the group is objectively wrong or contrary to the individual's private belief. Conformity is a fundamental social dynamic. It enables coordination and consensus but can also suppress dissent and enable groupthink.

Solomon Asch's experiments in the nineteen fifties revealed that people conform to obviously incorrect group judgments about line lengths roughly one-third of the time, even when alone they judge correctly. This was a startling demonstration of social influence. Conformity intensifies with group size, up to a point, unanimity with perfect consensus, and task ambiguity when the correct answer is unclear. It weakens dramatically when even one person dissents from the group consensus.

Normative conformity, going along to gain approval and avoid rejection, differs fundamentally from informational conformity, accepting the group's judgment as factually true when uncertain. Irving Janis developed the concept of groupthink, suppressed dissent in highly cohesive groups, which can lead to catastrophic decisions like the Bay of Pigs invasion or the Pearl Harbor surprise when conformity pressure overrides critical thinking.

Conformity varies significantly across cultures. Individualist societies like the USA and Western Europe show more dissent-tolerance and debate, while collectivist societies in East Asia and Africa typically value group harmony, face-saving, and consensus more. Conformity operates through social punishment—ostracism, ridicule, exclusion—and psychological mechanisms like uncertainty reduction, desire for belonging, and identity affiliation with the group.

Resistance to conformity requires either high confidence in one's judgment, prior commitment to nonconformity as an identity, or presence of an ally who also dissents. Online conformity operates through digital mechanisms like upvote and downvote systems, algorithmic amplification, and social media likes, which make group consensus visible and intensify normative pressure in new ways.
